speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the real estate sector, estate agents, salespersons and developers play an important role in detecting and deterring illicit activities, alongside financial institutions, lawyers, and law practice entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Over the years, we have established a robust risk management framework for the real estate sector, guided by the recommendations made by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: FATF sets international standards to tackle money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This Bill is part of our continuing efforts to bolster our ability to detect and deter such illicit activities within the real estate sector, thereby reinforcing our commitment to stamp out the laundering of criminal proceeds and financing of illicit activities through Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will take Members through the key amendments in these three key areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first set of amendments strengthens our penalty frameworks to strengthen the deterrent effect of our current regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, estate agents and salespersons are required to perform duties in relation to countering money laundering and terrorism financing activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Examples include the requirement to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) measures by salespersons on their clients.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Currently, non-compliant estate agents and salespersons may be subject to a financial penalty of up to $5,000 per case under the Council for Estate Agencies’ (CEA’s) Letter of Censure disciplinary regime for minor breaches.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Estate agents and salespersons who commit more serious breaches may face disciplinary action before a Disciplinary Committee, which is an independent tribunal comprising members from CEA’s Disciplinary Panel.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These members are from various backgrounds such as practising solicitors, architects, engineers or individuals from the real estate agency industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Disciplinary Committee may impose a financial penalty of up to $200,000 per case on estate agents or $100,000 per case on salespersons.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, the current penalty framework which allows financial penalties to be imposed on a per case basis does not provide sufficient deterrence.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is because the potential monetary benefits that estate agents and salespersons might obtain for facilitating illicit transactions could be significantly higher than the maximum financial penalty of $200,000 for estate agents, or $100,000 for salespersons.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Assuming that a salesperson facilitates the sale of one such property valued at, say, $10 million, a 2% commission for such a transaction would amount to $200,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When such financial gains far exceed the current maximum penalties for these offences, there is a clear need to raise the penalties for stronger deterrence.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Estate agents and salespersons who contravene any legislation or provision of a code of practice, ethics and conduct relating to money laundering, terrorism financing or proliferation financing, will now be subjected to a maximum penalty of up to $5,000 per contravention under CEA’s Letter of Censure regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For cases heard by the Disciplinary Committee, errant estate agents and salespersons will be subjected to a maximum penalty of up to $200,000 and $100,000 per contravention for estate agents and salespersons respectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Maximum penalties for other disciplinary breaches will remain on a per case basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Assume an errant salesperson has committed four disciplinary breaches that are referred to a Disciplinary Committee to be heard.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Of these breaches, two concern anti-money laundering obligations and the other two concern the salesperson’s negligence in handling a transaction.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Based on the existing penalty framework, the maximum financial penalty that can be imposed for all four breaches is $100,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the new penalty framework, the maximum financial penalty that can be imposed is now $300,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For the two breaches of anti-money laundering obligations, a maximum of $200,000 in financial penalties can be imposed as each breach is now subjected to a maximum of $100,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As for the two breaches of professional misconduct, an aggregate maximum financial penalty of $100,000 applies.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The amendments in this Bill will also enhance the composition framework for developers.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similar to estate agents and salespersons, developers are required to perform duties to counter money laundering and terrorism financing activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Currently, for less serious offences, non-compliant housing developers may be offered composition of up to $5,000 under the Housing Developers Control and Licensing Act (HDCLA).

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, this is significantly lower than the maximum fine for money laundering and terrorism financing offences, at $100,000 per offence upon conviction.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This means that the maximum composition sums for some offences will be increased to $50,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similar to the HDCLA, the maximum composition sum under the SCPA will be up to 50% of the maximum fine prescribed for the offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With these amendments, the approach for the maximum composition sums for money laundering and terrorism financing offences in the HDCLA and SCPA will be aligned with that of other sectors, such as precious stones and metal dealers.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The second set of amendments further align our regulatory regime with international standards set by the FATF.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Currently, estate agents and salespersons are only required to conduct due diligence measures on their own clients.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Hence, in transactions where either the buyer or seller are not represented by estate agents and salespersons, property-related due diligence measures may not be conducted on the buyer or seller who is unrepresented.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In recent years, FATF has also updated its standards to clearly set out the standards to identify, assess and mitigate risks associated with the financing of proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, or proliferation financing in short.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clauses 3 to 5, 12, 14, 15 and 17 of the Bill thus update the regulatory regime for estate agents, salespersons and developers to cover proliferation financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is similar to the relevant legislative frameworks for other sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The amendments to the composition regime for developers in clauses 13 and 16 of the bill would also allow proliferation financing related offences to be compounded.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, developers are required to assess whether a purchaser is designated as a terrorist or terrorist entity under relevant lists, or sanctioned by the United Nations.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If so, developers are required to decline to enter into or terminate transactions with the potential purchaser, and report the matter to the Police.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The amendments will make clear that this also applies to purchasers who are on the designated or sanction lists due to terrorism financing and proliferation financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These measures for terrorism financing and proliferation financing are generally not new to estate agents, salespersons and developers.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such measures are already part of existing anti-money laundering requirements as the underlying terrorism financing and proliferation financing offences are also money laundering predicate offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Efforts to combat terrorism financing and proliferation financing are also already part of the current measures performed by estate agents, salespersons and developers.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We now come to the third set of amendments which are clarifications to restrictions against persons convicted of money laundering, terrorism financing or proliferation financing offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similarly, clauses 12 and 15 of the Bill amend the HDCLA and SCPA respectively to clarify that money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing offences include offences under the law of any foreign country or territory.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In this way, persons convicted of such offences regardless of where they are committed will be subjected to prohibitions against becoming a housing developer, becoming a substantial shareholder, or holding a responsible position in a developer or in substantial shareholders of a developer.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: CEA and the Urban Redevelopment Authority will disseminate more information on these upcoming amendments to the real estate sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This Bill aligns the real estate sector with international standards and is another step in strengthening our national strategy against money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As criminals get more sophisticated over time, we will continue to remain vigilant and will not hesitate to tighten our regime further where necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a society, we must also remain watchful and vigilant.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Countering money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing in the real estate sector requires a concerted effort not just by the Government, but all stakeholders, such as businesses and individuals.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This collective partnership is key to our continued efforts to act decisively to detect and deter such illicit activities, while ensuring that our financial and business ecosystem remains reputable and trusted, and continues to thrive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: According to the Explanatory Statement, this is based on recommendations of FATF.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fighting money laundering is clearly an important matter, especially in a financial centre like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The recent arrests related to the multi-billion dollar money laundering cases in Singapore also highlighted that a number of those involved had used their ill-gotten gains for the purchase of properties in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, it is understandable that we would want to impose obligations on real estate agents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Their income is based on commissions and is generally irregular, depending on whether or not they have transactions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It also expands the existing obligations to cover counterparties to transactions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the test is phrased subjectively, I expect in practice, they will be judged objectively on whether or not they would have had reason to suspect money laundering.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, there will be a perverse incentive on agents to turn a blind eye – the infamous Nelsonian blindness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means in a situation where a normal person would suspect there might be money laundering, it is likely an agent would be expected to do so as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, due diligence obligations exist on banks and on law firms, who have to be especially careful when they take in client monies for conveyancing transactions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also take the Minister's point that they do apply to real estate agents as well – at least, in recent years, I think since 2021.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This actually already creates quite a secure backdrop to limit money laundering in property transactions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Essentially, if a party takes a loan or pays through a bank account, the bank would already have done due diligence or should have done due diligence on the source of funds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If instead of going to a bank, the person brings a pile of cash to his conveyancing lawyer's office, the lawyer would then clearly have their obligations triggered.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also be grateful if the Minister can clarify whether estate agents have had any issues complying with existing 2021 regulations, including obligations such as keeping records.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My main concern with expanding legislation is compared to banks and law firms, estate agents have more limited resources to conduct due diligence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is unsurprising, given the big ticket nature of real estate transactions and the sky high prices of our housing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it just underscores the importance of enhancing our regulatory efforts in the sector to prevent a recurrence of the events of August 2023.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For this reason, there is little reason to reject legislative effort – changes that edify such efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the importance of the issue, I was therefore surprised to see how the proposed amendments did not appear to be all that extensive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many of them entail logical, but seemingly minor expansions of scope from changing the term "money laundering and terrorism financing" to money laundering, proliferation, financing and terrorism financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, by my count, half of the clauses in the Bill relate to this change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I do not necessarily question the value of enfolding the illicit financing of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) into the scope of our anti-money laundering regime, it would nevertheless be helpful to this House to understand why this definition or expansion is deemed to be so crucial and relevant for our continued efforts in the real estate sector at this particular point in time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: How many of the recent cases that have come under investigation have involved the financing of WMDs relative to plain vanilla AML or terrorism financing?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Based on my reading, the remaining provisions introduced are also somewhat fairly mild.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is only in clause 10 where there seems at first glance to be some real teeth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It proposes amendments to the regulation making powers of the Council in section 72 of the Estate Agents Act, but when one returns to the original Act, one may be disappointed again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here the change is again to be to insert "proliferation financing" to the list of requirements for what may be subject to regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Council for Estate Agencies in its guide on 2021 regulations related to the prevention of money laundering and terrorism financing had already set out a comprehensive set of guidelines for how to conduct customer due diligence, including enhanced procedures for when the risk of money laundering or terrorism financing is greater.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The January 2025 version of the guide does indeed update the list of red flag indicators, doubling the page coverage in process, but my point is simply that we will not be raft of laws to combat so-called Singapore-washing even before this present update.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Inter-Ministerial Committee report observed this too, noting that the, and I quote, "uneven implementation practices across and within sectors".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And in response to this clarification question that I had posed on the Inter-Ministerial Committee last year, Minister Indranee conceded that the Government had, and I quote, "already started to do more in this space and will certainly see what they can do to strengthen the regulations in the sector".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the relevant question beyond whether these changes proposed in today's Bill are only marginal is whether more substantive legislation is actually required to bring the industry to the frontier of AML best practices than the rest of the financial sector in Singapore is required to abide by.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am not a lawyer, but I would appreciate if the Minister would be willing to share if the laws, as they stand, together with the amendments proposed today are indeed sufficient to have brought about an earlier detection and detention of the Fujian Gang.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, was it a matter of execution that fell short rather than the legal framework per se?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if not, what laws would be necessary?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And why have these laws not been proposed to this House today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The essence of my message, Sir, is simple.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do not believe that we actually lack the laws necessary to investigate, apprehend and prosecute egregious money-laundering practices in the real estate sector.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill also has some important initiatives towards safeguarding our real estate market from illicit financial flows.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While Singapore must remain open for business, it must also be a place that is hostile to money launderers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill reflects that balance – fortifying our defenses while preserving confidence in our institutions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill also introduces stricter licensing criteria which is very important to protect the integrity of the sector.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It provides businesses with the space to understand, prepare for, and adapt to the new requirements.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Implementing these new requirements will mean higher operational costs for all.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Estate agencies and property developers may need to hire more compliance professionals, invest in new technology and restructure internal processes to meet reporting obligations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: I now have six clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: One, while the Bill addresses proliferation financing, it would be useful to clarify how this concept specifically applies to estate agents and property developers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: For instance, how will transactions involving foreign buyers be monitored for potential links to such financing and what specific indicators or red flags should agents look out for?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Two, will digital property platforms involved in cross-border transactions fall under the same compliance regime.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: It would be helpful to understand how enforcement will be operationalised in these more complex situations, providing stakeholders with reassurance and confidence in the regulatory process.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Three, this Bill introduces stricter obligations, but stakeholders may need more clarity on the level of verification required, especially in complex commercial property transactions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: It would be helpful to specify the legal obligations and liabilities when a client refuses to provide due diligence documentation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Clarity on whether penalties will be calibrated based on business size or intent would ensure that SMEs are not disproportionately impacted by unintentional lapses.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Five, this Bill aims to align with FATF's recommendations, but estate agents and developers may need more guidance on handling transactions involving foreign jurisdictions that do not have equivalent AML/CFT standards.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: It would be important to consider how stricter checks might affect legitimate foreign investment.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: What strategies will be employed to ensure that the enhanced compliance measures do not deter investment flows, thereby maintaining Singapore’s appeal as a financial hub?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Lastly, while the Bill outlines the need for compliance, businesses would benefit from a more structured transitional support.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Beyond the implementation window, what forms of assistance – such as grants, digital compliance tools or subsidised training – are planned to help businesses operationalise these requirements efficiently?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Such support will be crucial, especially for SMEs navigating the new regulatory landscape.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Strengthening due diligence, tightening enforcement, and embracing global standards affirms our position as a responsible, forward-looking financial hub.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: But as we raise the bar, we must also bring our businesses – especially the smaller ones – along with us.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: The regulatory net must be tight, but not so tangled that it stifles legitimate activity or innovation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I rise in support of the Anti-Money Laundering and Other Matters (Estate Agents and Developers) Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the key provisions of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But I have some questions and would like to seek clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will these guidelines be tailored to address the unique challenges within the real estate sector?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government ensure that all stakeholders will be adequately prepared for the compliance system?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Smaller agencies may face resource constraints in sending their staff for training and implementing compliance measures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What support mechanisms will be in place to assist them in meeting the new regulatory requirements?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does the government plan to monitor compliance with these new regulations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another pertinent issue is that of inter-Ministry and agency collaboration.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the complexity of money laundering schemes, how will various government agencies collaborate to ensure a cohesive and effective approach to enforcement? : Finally, it is about public awareness.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Beyond the real estate sector, what efforts will be made to educate the general public about these challenges to foster a culture of vigilance against money laundering?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By addressing the vulnerabilities within the real estate sector, we have taken a decisive step to safeguard our reputation as a global financial centre.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I look forward to the deliberations on this Bill and the collaborative efforts to ensure its effective implementation.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, are you speaking on this Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Strengthening our defences against financial crime is a critical national priority.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I commend the Government's efforts to align our regulations with the recommendations of FATF.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill represents a significant step forward in safeguarding our financial system and housing market from exploitation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, while I applaud the intent behind this legislation, I have several clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The additional compliance costs imposed by this Bill, particularly regarding counterparty due diligence under clause 6, section 44BA, could prove disproportionately challenging.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If these smaller players are overburdened, it could stifle their growth or even drive them out of business entirely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would reduce competition and limit consumer choice within the already big-company-dominated real estate market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, the lack of expertise and resources among smaller estate agents could result in higher compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This may ultimately be passed on to consumers or salespeople.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that this legislation does not inadvertently create an uneven playing field, where only large firms have the capacity to absorb these new obligations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be financial support or training subsidies available to smaller agencies to ensure they do not unintentionally fall afoul of these new regulations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, will resources be made available to smaller firms when dealing with foreign clients?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that they are able to perform due diligence without being penalised due to limited means?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards are in place to prevent large firms from passing on their increased compliance costs to smaller subcontractors or resellers, thereby exacerbating the burden?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While robust regulations are essential, they are meaningless without effective mechanisms to ensure adherence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If enforcement is weak or overly focused on procedural matters, bad actors will inevitably find ways to circumvent the rules, while legitimate businesses continue to shoulder the burden of compliance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot allow this law to become a paper tiger – compliance on paper must translate into effective enforcement in practice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or will enforcement remain largely reactive, relying on reports rather than proactive investigation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does this Bill, beyond increasing reporting requirements, actively improve the detection of real estate transactions linked to illicit funds?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What proactive measures are being implemented to identify deceitful activities and prevent them before they occur?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What key performance indicators (KPIs) will be used to assess its effectiveness?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is success determined by the number of fines collected, the number of cases prosecuted or, more importantly, by a reduction in real estate-related financial crime?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, addressing financial crime in the real estate sector is not solely the responsibility of estate agents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Consumers, including buyers, sellers, landlords, tenants and developers, must also be aware of their role in preventing illicit transactions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While estate agencies must enforce strict controls, property owners themselves have a duty to conduct their own checks and declarations, particularly in cases like harboring illicit funds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The policy should incorporate strong consumer education efforts to ensure that all parties involved in a real estate transaction understand their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, what measures are in place to enhance consumer education about financial crime risks in real estate transactions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government ensure their buyers, sellers and landlords are equipped with the knowledge to detect and report suspicious activities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has witnessed several high-profile cases highlighting vulnerabilities in our current system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The impact on the real estate market was significant, with at least 105 properties facing prohibition of disposal orders, and at least 54 properties liquidated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This underscores the urgent need for enhanced due diligence and stricter enforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ensure this Bill achieves its intended goals, we must adopt a balanced approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, we need targeted support for small estate agents so they are not disproportionately burdened by compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, enforcement must be robust and proactive, not just a box-ticking exercise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is a critical step in the right direction, but its effectiveness will depend on thoughtful implementation and ongoing industry engagement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us work together to ensure that while we strengthen our defences against financial crime, we do not unintentionally weaken the competitiveness and sustainability of our real estate industry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Minister to take these concerns into serious consideration and to put in place the necessary safeguards and support measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us send a clear message that Singapore remains a place of integrity, fairness and accountability in real estate transactions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Vikram Nair asked how this Bill improves the detection of real estate transactions linked to illicit funds and whether the additional obligations are necessary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, licensed estate agents, registered salespersons and developers are mandated to perform a robust set of customer due diligence measures on the clients they represent or purchasers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, a buyer or seller who is unrepresented by an estate agent or salesperson may not be covered by such due diligence measures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will strengthen our regulatory and governance framework, and help to ensure more timely detection and prevention of illicit activities within the real estate sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee, Mr Neil Parekh and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how we will support the real estate sector in meeting these requirements, especially salespersons and smaller estate agents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Neil Parekh also asked how estate agents, salespersons and developers can better monitor transactions that may be related to proliferation financing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All estate agents, salespersons and developers are familiar with how these checks should be done, as they are already required to conduct such measures on their own clients or purchasers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For estate agents and salespersons specifically, the relevant content on the required due diligence measures is covered in the courses for new salespersons and continuing professional development courses for existing salespersons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To further support our estate agents and salespersons in meeting these obligations, we will be stepping up on training.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CEA has also set out clear guidelines on how customer due diligence measures should be done, including providing indicators of potential high-risk or suspicious transactions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CEA will update its resource webpage to put out more comprehensive information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This webpage will also be updated regularly to factor in new threats or vulnerabilities that arise over time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To support smaller players, one of the industry associations in the real estate agency industry, namely the Singapore Estate Agents Association (SEAA), also provides subsidised access to commercial screening services, which its members can subscribe to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We share Mr Don Wee's concern of a compliance burden on legitimate businesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng already raised the issue of how we will ensure that compliance costs are manageable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the degree of checks required varies based on the assessed risk profile of the purchaser or client.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) and CEA had also consulted the industry and took their feedback into account when developing the requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our consultation included major estate agents, industry associations that represent many small and mid-sized estate agents and developers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Stakeholders understood the need for the changes and were supportive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked if the existing regime covers digital property platforms and cross-border transactions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Regarding digital property platforms, if an entity only publishes advertisements or disseminates information and does not perform work that constitutes estate agency work, it will not be subject to the requirements of the Estate Agents Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Concerning developers, the Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act and Sale of Commercial Properties Act cover all developers regulated by URA, including cross-border transactions and transactions on digital property platforms by these developers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On Mr Don Wee's question on how the Government plans to monitor compliance with these new regulations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: During such inspections, CEA and URA check if the appropriate due diligence measures were performed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CEA and URA also conduct ad hoc inspections based on information from other law enforcement agencies, whistle-blowers or complaints received on possible infringements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We share Mr Neil Parekh's view on the need to maintain Singapore's appeal to legitimate foreign investors while enforcing stricter checks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Having a strong system and measures in place to combat money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing provides certainty and makes our business environment more robust and attractive to foreign investors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this regard, CEA and URA adopt a risk-based approach when conducting inspections.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, estate agents, salespersons and developers that are identified to be of higher risk are prioritised for inspections and subject to more regular inspections.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such risk factors include the customer profile and type of property being purchased or sold.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked what the obligations and liabilities of estate agents and developers are, if a client or purchaser refuses to provide necessary due diligence documents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the penalties that will be imposed for non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked if penalties will be calibrated based on the size of the business or intent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The key changes to the penalty framework are as per what I had set out in my opening speech.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Contraventions of anti-money laundering obligations are assessed based on the facts and circumstances of each case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would not be appropriate to calibrate penalties based on company size.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CEA and URA will share the revised guidelines and implementation details in advance of that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how we would measure the effectiveness of the proposals in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Potential indications will include the number of severe cases that have been averted due to the existence of this latest set of requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Members Mr Don Wee and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked what efforts will be made to educate the general public about the changes in this Bill and to foster a culture of vigilance against money laundering.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The ongoing efforts by URA, CEA and law enforcement agencies will continue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include educating homebuyers on the need to provide information to facilitate customer due diligence measures, and outreach efforts to the wider society through digital posters on money laundering risks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, Mr Don Wee asked how Government agencies collaborate to ensure a cohesive and effective approach to countering money laundering.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked what proactive measures are being implemented to identify deceitful activities and prevent them before they occur.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether CEA is equipped to deal with evolving money laundering threats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The close partnership between Government agencies ensures that agencies, like CEA and URA, can tap on the various inter-agency platforms to share intelligence, detect suspicious activities and coordinate enforcement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I turn, now, to the points raised by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and let me just check my records and my notes of what he said.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If I can summarise, essentially, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggested that the changes or the amendments in this Bill do not appear to go very far.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But at the same time, he, in a sense, actually answered his own question because he said he assumed that the underlying reason for the seemingly limited state of affairs is that we have an already robust regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's starting point is correct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have a very robust regime and that is the reason why we were able to crack that $3 billion money laundering case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But that said, it is clearly not perfect, and we felt, after that, that it was necessary to see what the gaps were and how we could further strengthen an already strong regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, there were two points that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He asked about the inclusion of proliferation financing, suggesting that this appeared to be an add-on that did not take things very far.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, the enhancement of penalties which also did not appear to be big moves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer to that is, actually, I think, maybe Assoc Prof Lim may have missed the bigger picture.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The bigger picture being this, first, on proliferation financing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, I said, "This Bill seeks to strengthen current penalty frameworks and to further align our regulatory regime with FATF standards and then to make miscellaneous amendments to clarify certain things." So, that second point, "aligning our regulatory regime with FATF standards".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The old FATF standards dealt with money laundering and countering terrorism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the reason for these amendments is because FATF updated its recommendations to member countries to include mitigation of proliferation financing risks and we are, therefore, updating our legislation to align with the FATF standards.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that takes care of the proliferation financing part.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the much bigger picture is this, and Assoc Prof Lim actually did refer to it in the course of his speech, which was, he said, and this is again exactly correct, that the amendments in this Bill are actually pursuant to the recommendations of the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Anti-Money Laundering, which I co-chaired with various other Ministers of State.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And under that report, which is available on the MAS website, there was a whole slew of measures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, it started out by explaining our already strong system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, it talked about the recommendations that we were making and there were three key broad categories falling under the headings of "Prevent", "Detect" and "Enforce".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And under prevention and detection, there was a wide range of measures in the report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I hope that that addresses the question that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The question is, "That the Bill be now read a Second time."

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I believe Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has a clarification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I wish to state for the record, I have no quarrel with the proposed amendments to the existing regime, which is why I supported the Bill and I do believe that they will make it stronger, at least on paper.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But the matter in question, if you will, is a question that I also posed in my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Would any of the clauses in the current Bill have helped us to potentially apprehend the Fujian Gang any sooner and if not, is the Government implicitly saying that there were indeed no lapses during the incident that we could have learnt from, that would have been identified by the Inter-Ministerial Committee that we could not have put into the legislation being debated today?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am not sure that the question actually gels, because I think the question is whether any of the clauses would have helped us to catch them sooner.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim is talking about is the prevention and actually, more importantly, the detection portion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this one deals with the penalties, the review of the penalties.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moving back to the "detect" portion, that was not really so much a matter of legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the provision in these Bills are not really aimed at the detection portion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And as I mentioned earlier, actually, this was dealt with in the Ministerial Statements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because we explained that the agencies were tracking them for some time and then only took action, I think, several months or maybe almost a year later because they wanted to make sure they caught everybody in the net.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, were there things that could be strengthened in order to assist with detection?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is yes, because no system is perfect and that is set out in the Inter-Ministerial Committee report as to how to be able to better detect and that includes various measures, including making the individuals in various sectors part of our gatekeepers and part of the system, hence helping and educating them to be able to identify suspicious transactions earlier and also training them on filing Suspicious Transaction Reports.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Are there any more clarifications for the Minister?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: If not, I shall pose the question.  .    .
